No, I mean something else by that. Let me rephrase it. There is more going on than meets the eye. Some things are going on behind the scenes. By live debate 1 mean an evolving debate, and the issue is continuing. The Minister said during Question Period that he had been talking to his British Columbia counterpart just before Question Period. There is action, if you like, going on between the federal and provincial Ministers, as there should be. NDP, Liberal and Conservative Members of Parliament are participating, using whatever connections they have with their provincial counterparts. For example, we can put pressure on the NDP Leader in British Columbia to bring him on board. Our Conservative friends can put some pressure on through some of their Social Credit friends in B.C. The Speaker of the House of Commons cannot participate in this matter but people know that he has a deep-felt interest in the environment. He has colleagues and friends in British Columbia who are not without influence and who are deeply committed to this issue. These are Conservatives who are deeply committed to environmental issues. There was a dinner party for the Speaker in Vancouver about a month and a half ago. 1 had the privilege to attend and 1 met many people who were not of my political persuasion. Yet 1 could see they were deeply committed to environmental matters.
1 say this to the Government of British Columbia: There is a big constituency out there of all Parties who want to see a solution to this problem.
We are moving. The Government of British Columbia announced that it will no longer require a 10-year period of logging on South Moresby. That makes sense because if you had 10 years of logging, there would not be many trees left. We are making progress even as we speak in this debate. That is what 1 mean when I say it is a live debate.
This issue is also important because it tells us what kind of Canada we are setting up and where we are going. I had a chance to speak the other day with a person who works in Ottawa for the European Economic Community. They have an office here. 1 talked to him and he said to me: "I love being in Canada". 1 asked why. We have lots of problems, unemployment-, we do not own our own industry, sometimes I feel we are a colony of the U.S. He said: "No, I like it here because this is a civilized country". It is nice to hear the view of an outsider. I think what he would say in this debate is that to save South Moresby Island and create a national park would make us a more civilized country.
This debate has been going on for a while. I would not be human if I did not point out that on May 2, 1980, I had the privilege of introducing a Private Members' Bill in this House, Bill C-454, an Act respecting a national park on Moresby Island and its adjacent islands. I was not the only one. Later on my colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena, introduced Bill C-45. He basically took my Bill and got all the geography right where 1 made mistakes. This Bill was one way of keeping the debate going in those years. I just want to read the following from the explanatory notes of Bill C-454:
This bill would authorize the Governor in Council to set aside, as a National Park of Canada, any lands on Moresby Island.
The southern portion of Moresby Island is internationally recognized as an outstanding biological, geographical, and cultural area.
The coastline has exposure to both Hecate Strait and the open Pacific, with a rich variety of shorelines including sea caves, sandy beaches, tidal falls, hidden coves, shallow reefs, and safe anchorages. The area contains a remarkable variety of intact ecological systems ranging from the San Cristoval alpine environment to the fresh water Victoria Lakes and from the Skincuttle Inlet marine gardens to the bonsai forest of Gowgaia Bay.
Moresby Island is home of the world's largest subspecies of black bear and the rare Peale's Peregrine Falcon. The unusual salt marshes are part of the migratory flyway of the Pacific Coast, and there are numerous highly productive salmon streams. The virgin rain forests of the area have Canada's largest and tallest Red Cedar, Sitka Spruce and Western Hemlock.
Moresby Island was inhabited by the Haida Indians until the last century, and includes numerous archaeological and village sites. Most remarkable is the assemblage of carved cedar totems found on Anthony Island, the best remaining example of a traditional west coast native village.
I read that to give you some idea of what the territory is like there. Have you ever seen that picture of the falling poles in the rain forest? Some poles are falling down and others are tilted and so on. That is Anthony Island. That is a beautiful sight.
I said the Hon. Member for Skeena followed this up with Bill C-45. On August 29, 1981, the UN declared some world heritage sites. One site was the Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta and the other was Anthony Island in British Columbia.
I quote from the press release of the Minister of the Environment as follows:
The Unesco World Heritage Convention, a treaty among more than 60 nations, recognizes that the world's natural and cultural heritage transcends national boundaries and must be identified, protected and preserved for future generations. The Pyramids of Giza, Egypt; Chartres Cathedral, France; the ancient city of Damascus, Syrian Arab Republic; the historic centre of Rome, Italy; the Galapagos Islands, Ecuador; Sagarmatha (Mount Everest) National Park, Nepal; and Yellowstone National Park, U.S.A. are among the other World Heritage Sites.
They also mentioned the Great Barrier Reef, the Palace and Park at Fontainebleau, France, and the Old City of Jerusalem. South Moresby, as a world heritage site, fits in with these places in the rest of the world, which I think we would all agree need to be preserved and protected. This is what we are fighting for today.
There has been a long and noble campaign. My friend and colleague, Murray Rankin, a professor of law at the University of Victoria, wrote in The Globe and Mail of July 26, 1979, about the battle raging to preserve rare wilderness from the axe. The Western Canada Wilderness Committee led by Paul George, an environmentalist from British Columbia, has tried to preserve the area. It presented petitions to Parliament and made posters and buttons, mostly out of their own pockets. These were not rich people and they paid for this mostly out of their own pockets. This campaign has inspired people. I received a letter from a young man in Peterborough in 1981. He said:
May 14, 1987

Last summer I had the opportunity to spend a month kayaking through the South Moresby wilderness in the Queen Charlottes, and subsequently have become very interested and actively concerned about the fate of this magnificent area. In addition to working on slide shows, distributing literature, etc, I have been working on a term paper focusing in on the social, economic and environmental issues underlying the controversy.
That is the kind of thing I am talking about, young Canadians kayaking up in the wilderness. The Western Canada Wilderness Committee sent me a letter on February 14, 1981, which indicates how many Members of Parliament supported my Bill in principle, how many did not support it, and how many were non-committal. They kept the pressure up, and 1 thank them for that. There was interest right across the country from Newfoundland to Peterborough and to British Columbia. They did not have much money, only a lot of determination.
I cited the Berger report called Northern Frontier, Northern Homeland earlier in my question to the Minister. I have already described how Justice Berger talked about the native rights and how self-determination meant being more Canadian rather than less Canadian. Through this report Judge Berger was trying to show that there were different interests, a frontier interest as well as a homeland interest. This is part of the homeland of the native people.
Often southern Canadians, if you like, look at the North and rural areas as big, empty areas which we can exploit. We forget that they are people's backyards. We should always try to remember that. When I am flying over northern Canada I try to remember that that is not just a big, empty land, but people's backyards. If we can think of it that way we can understand how the native people feel about it.
I was lucky to be in Banff on Tuesday. I went for a little walk and literally ran into some of the magnificent animals in that park. I thought of how lucky we are to have that national park.
These are difficult issues. They are not motherhood issues. There are different interests. As I said earlier, loggers have an interest and have to be accommodated. We must deal with tourist operators. We must weigh matters and cannot leave any group out. Our concept of Canada is that no one is left out, that everyone is encouraged. We will not leave the loggers out, but for the sake of 50 or 100 jobs we must think of what weighs against it. On the other side is the preservation of a most magnificent site for future generations.
I am confident that the Minister, helped by Members of the House from all Parties, can find a way to do this. This resolution will be passed tpday. By a rather unusual procedural measure we are going to agree to pass this motion as the view of the House.
I want to ask Premier Vander Zalm and his Cabinet to find a way to make an agreement on this matter. If they can make an agreement, they will be applauded by many, many people in British Columbia and in all of Canada. I think this can be accomplished. The Minister's participation and actions today should be applauded. For future generations we can establish a
Supply
magnificent park in that area which some day will be part of our national parks system of which Canadians can be proud and we can have a very civilized country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 82-DESIGNATION OF SOUTH MORESBY AREA AS NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to join with those who have commended the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for presenting this motion to the House today. His speech in support of this motion ranks among the best that I have heard given in the House of Commons. While I am handing out bouquets, I think the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) also made important and significant contributions to this debate.
The motion of the Hon. Member for Skeena proposes a specific plan for South Moresby. It does not say, although I would argue that it is implicit within it, that the Queen Charlotte Islands, and South Moresby in particular, are part of a very important unsettled aboriginal claim.
The Queen Charlotte Islands are the hereditary lands of the Haida people. These lands are called by them the "land of Haida" or "beautiful islands". South Moresby, as a part of the Queen Charlottes, is both a unique and a very fascinating part of Canada. I am happy that I had the opportunity to visit those islands when my daughter was a resident there.
South Moresby is a part of the Haida lands which they claim have been in their possession for thousands of years. South Moresby contains, as others have noted, the highest concentration of endemic plants, birds, mammals and insects of any area of its size in all of North America. As well, there are major archaeological sites in South Moresby as a part of those Haida lands. So valuable and so important are these archaeological sites that certain responsible citizens in Canada who have the necessary knowledge and required expertise to make these judgments went to the United Nations and asked that South Moresby be declared a world heritage site.
One will find on South Moresby primeval forests containing western red cedar, yellow cedar, western hemlock and Sitka spruce which are among the largest of their genera. However, I am entering this debate today not only in support of the fact that South Moresby is unique and of great environmental significance. 1 recognize that and appreciate it. Other Members more competent in the environmental area than I can claim to be have spoken eloquently on that point.
I want to use the time allocated to me in this debate to talk about another matter of equal importance. It is that we are discussing today the homeland of the Haida Indian people. As the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development noted in his speech, since 1973 our nation has had a policy that recognizes that some Indian people have outstanding aboriginal rights or claims. These are claims that were never dealt with by way of treaty or by way of any other kind of agreement which is binding and legal.

May 14, 1987
Supply
This policy was given birth as a result of a Supreme Court decision rendered in 1973. It was the case brought to the Supreme Court by the Nishga Indian people of British Columbia. The particular case is known as the Calder case. In that case, six out of seven judges agreed that the Nishga people had an aboriginal title in accord with English law and that they had this at the time of the first contact with Europeans. However, the six judges split three to three as to whether that title still existed. There was one judge who opted out of the decision altogether, so that the Nishga people lost their case on a technicality.
But all was not lost. The Prime Minister of the day, Mr. Trudeau, who had strongly resisted for a long period of time the legal and valid concept of aboriginal rights, became persuaded otherwise as a result of that case. I remember well the day that he spoke on the issue from a different point of view. It was one of the important historic moments during which I have been here in the Parliament of Canada.
As a result of that, the federal Government decided to acknowledge the principle that aboriginal rights still existed today and the Government committed itself to negotiate those claims with the Indian people. That claims policy, with some recent and welcome modifications-although the Minister and I agreed they are modest in their scope-is still in effect today.
Today we talk about aboriginal rights, aboriginal claims, and aboriginal title. When you and I first came to Parliament, Mr. Speaker, it would have been a strange debate to hear anyone present these arguments. Today, parliamentarians understand them and Canadian citizens in growing numbers have an appreciation of what is involved.
1 want to submit, however, that we are very close to another important breakthrough. I hope that I am here long enough to see it happen. That breakthrough is to appreciate fully and adequately what is involved in aboriginal title.
I have had some delightful and interesting discussions in the Committee on Aboriginal Affairs with officials and others about the meaning of aboriginal title. For example, very recently I asked one senior official: "I get the impression from what you said to the members of the committee that you consider aboriginal title to be some sort of a burden or some sort of interest that exists on the Crown rights". He agreed that that is the way he interpreted it, but the question that has not yet been resolved in Canada is when the Crown right took precedent over aboriginal title.
How can we make the assumption that the Crown right exists and there is some sort of lien, called an aboriginal title, on the Crown right? In response to these kinds of questions, the senior official agreed with me. He said that, first, he has to work in somewhat limited confines and has to work within what the courts have told them. He said: "For example, the courts have not said as much as we might like about what aboriginal title is". This is interesting because it is so relevant to the debate today.
He went on to say that the courts will say a lot more because of the B.C. cases that are coming forward. It was his impression that all the courts have told them so far is that aboriginal title consists of hunting, fishing and gathering rights, traditional use rights over lands which the aboriginal people have continually occupied. I predict that we can expect very soon a major breakthrough on that limited understanding of aboriginal title. Aboriginal title is much more than that.
A curious process has been going on in Canada. Even if we live within these limited confines of what aboriginal title is, even then the aboriginal people of Canada are having difficulties with hunting, fishing and trapping. Those court cases will change the way we understand what aboriginal title means with respect to Crown rights.
The federal Government has now accepted 13 claims in British Columbia. Another seven claims are being examined by the Department of Justice.
The Haida formally submitted their claim to the federal Government in 1980. The Department of Justice formally accepted it as being valid for the purposes of negotiation in 1983. As the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development pointed out to the House earlier, the problem is that the Government of British Columbia is not willing to negotiate along with the Government of Canada in the settlement of this or any other claim in the Province of British Columbia. It continues to take the view of those three judges in the Calder case, who argued that aboriginal title had been extinguished. However, no one has yet been able to show the document, the historical or the legal evidence, that would prove that that extinguishment took place. That is why those court cases in British Columbia are so fascinating and will be so crucial in the settlement of aboriginal title.
I sincerely believe that the Government of British Columbia should follow the dictum of John F. Kennedy, who said at one time: "We shall never fear to negotiate but we shall never negotiate from fear".
We know that aboriginal claims in this country can be successfully and satisfactorily settled. There is no reason for fear on the part of other Canadians, on the part of Members of Parliament, or on the part of third party interests. There is no need to fear negotiation in the settlement of aboriginal claims.
I want to say how strongly I agree with what the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said in the House this afternoon. It is far better to negotiate those claims than to have them resolved by way of litigation. If the courts impose settlements because there has been a lack of political will to negotiate, then those settlements may be objectionable to many Canadians. Instead of bringing the kind of peace and harmony that we all want in all parts of Canada in living with the aboriginal people of this country, those kinds of settlements may cause irritation and disagreement. That is not the way we want to go.
May 14, 1987

I have said that the claims of the Haida people have been accepted by Canada. I want to say as well that the Province of British Columbia is a signatory to the Constitution Act of 1982. The Constitution Act of 1982 recognizes that aboriginal rights exist. They are contained in Section 35 of our Constitution. Those Premiers who have gone to the First Ministers' Conference and argued that Section 35 is nothing but an empty box are fooling themselves. That is self-delusion.
Section 35, asserting that aboriginal rights exist, is not an empty box. It is a full box. That is why, even though the last First Ministers' Conference on aboriginal rights seeking a definition did not succeed, the aboriginal leaders knew that they did not walk away empty-handed because Section 35 is still theirs. In time, we will begin to see all that is in Section 35.
There is a recognition of these rights. Since the Haida claim has been accepted, is it not only logical that there should be a postponement of any kind of development in that area which has been submitted as a claim for settlement by way of negotiation? Whether that development is cutting down trees, building roads or establishing new towns or mining, all that should be postponed until there is a just, fair and adequate settlement of this claim accepted by the Government of Canada after careful analysis by the Department of Justice.
For one brief moment, I believe, the Government of British Columbia was recognizing this important point. At one point it did impose a moratorium on logging on a part of South Moresby on Lyell Island. Then, to the surprise and dismay of the Haida people, that moratorium was suddenly lifted. Should any of us wonder why there was a strong protest from those people, and why that protest generated so much sympathy and understanding right across the country? People are not only concerned about the environmental aspects of South Moresby but about the other matter, which is the burden of my contribution to this debate today, and that is, that there is an unsettled claim.
As part of those negotiations in the settling of the Haida claim, I believe, as the motion today suggests, that there should be active consideration of setting aside the South Moresby area of the Queen Charlotte Islands as a national park reserve. I accept that. The Leader of my Party is a strong proponent of that idea. However, it is also my firm view and that of my Party that the full participation of the Haida people is an essential requirement in any decisions that are made, whether they are about national parks or about any other kind of economic development. I am not talking about consultation. Members of Parliament who know about aboriginal affairs will realize that consultation has become a dirty word in relations between the Government of Canada and the aboriginal people. It has become a dirty word because it has been abused. Consultation has been a sham. It has been play acting. It has not been real.
Supply
What I am calling for, as the motion suggests, is not mere consultation, but full participation and full collaboration of the Haida people in the settling of this claim. I believe, with Members of the House and the Minister who is working toward this end, that in a part of that settlement we will see a national park reserve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 82-DESIGNATION OF SOUTH MORESBY AREA AS NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join in this debate this afternoon. I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for bringing this question before the House, particularly at this time. As the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said, it is a rather lively debate in the sense that negotiations are going on hourly right at this time between the Minister's Department and the Government of British Columbia.
This is also a rather odd occasion, at least for me. 1 have been in this House for several years now and it is not very frequent that we have such wide unanimity on any issue. This is more like a love-in than a debate. Even before the debate got started, the House agreed it would pass this resolution unanimously. I think that is very peculiar and unusual happening, particularly with respect to a motion put by the Opposition.
I have no hesitation at all in endorsing the motion which calls for the Government of British Columbia to co-operate with the Government of Canada in setting aside an area in South Moresby as a national park reserve. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), as we all know, has been working for almost two years to achieve this objective.
Hon. Members will recall, I am sure, that one of the first public statements the Minister made in 1985 was a pledge to work for the establishment of a South Moresby National Park. Since that time he has met on many occasions with various representatives, particularly those from the Province of British Columbia, in order to work towards the goal of preserving one of the greatest natural wonders of our country for the benefit and enjoyment of Canadians, and the development of a world-class tourist attraction.
Hon. Members from every province and territory will certainly have first-hand knowledge of what a national park can do for Canada. There are national parks in every province, I believe, and they are certainly an outstanding example of what can be done to preserve the original territory. I think Canada takes second place to no country in preserving its national parks.
I believe one of the most famous national parks is the Pacific Rim National Park in British Columbia, it was the first national park on the West Coast of British Columbia. The agreement with respect to that park was signed in 1970. The lands of the famous Long Beach section of the park were transferred to the Government of Canada in 1972. In barely 15 years the Pacific Rim National Park has grown to be one of the most attractive and popular national parks in Canada. In the last two years alone more than a million visitors have

May 14, 1987
Supply
enjoyed the peace and beauty of the Pacific Rim National Park. Since the park first opened, over five million visitors have visited this natural wonderland. 1 am sure all of those visitors would gladly endorse the motion of the Hon. Member for Skeena. I myself, with my family, have visited that park on many occasions. I can assure Hon. Members that nowhere else have I seen a greater example of natural beauty preserved in a manner which is capable of being enjoyed by everyone without destroying the natural flora and fauna.
As the Minister said today during his speech and on many other occasions, national parks in Canada are not a frill. They are not peripheral to the Canadian experience. They are part of our heritage and part of our way of life. They are places where Canadians find refreshment, inspiration and renewal. In a world which is becoming increasingly smaller and more crowded our national parks serve the purpose of preserving the original face of Canada.
I join with the Minister and Hon. Members of this House to urge the Government of British Columbia to co-operate in setting aside the South Moresby National Park Reserve. This is a difficult question. As someone said, it is not a question of motherhood. For that reason, and as the Minister has recognized so eloquently in his speech, it is necessary we talk about parks and recognize the competing interests. These are valid and difficult questions. Therefore, I strongly endorse the proposal that the federal Government provide for compensation and share in the costs of those interests which will be affected by such a national park reserve. Nothing is free in this society, and the establishment of a park is certainly not free. There are people who will suffer economic loss as a result of establishing a park in this area. Those people should be compensated adequately for the loss they will suffer.
The Minister of the Environment has said we will put our cash where our commitment is-right on the barrel head. I agree with that. We will cost share the buying out of the timber rights. That is only just. Compensation is really not the issue. As the Minister has said, it is a matter of political courage, will and responsibility to ensure that if this park is created, and 1 hope it is, all parties concerned will find it to their benefit and that no one will suffer inordinately from its establishment.
1 understand, and it is only natural, that the province will seek the most favourable terms possible for the creation of such a park. I suggest that this is not a poker game in which someone is trying to gain an advantage over another. This is part of nation building. This park will be part of our nation for time immemorial. I honestly believe that while a fair price should be paid, no one particular party should benefit to the disadvantage of another. Therefore, 1 urge the Government of the Province of British Columbia to come to the negotiating table in search of a fair deal and not an unfair one. The key to this issue has to be the cost to the various parties concerned, and those are the costs of the Government. I think other
matters can be worked out. Hopefully they are well on their way to being worked out now. Excessive costs will be the first thing that will torpedo this tremendous idea.
An agreement between Canada and British Columbia to establish the final boundaries for the Pacific Rim National Park was signed in February of this year. That is 15 years from the time negotiations were first started. The Government of Canada has agreed to pay $25 million as its share of compensation for forest interests. All those who are interested in national parks were pleased that the federal Government finally resolved this long-standing issue. I congratulate the Minister for so doing. This is a clear signal that the federal Government in living up to its commitment to the province for the Pacific Rim Park was seeking and is seeking similar cooperation for the South Moresby proposal.
It is time for political courage. I share the concern of the provincial Government and of Members of the House with respect to protecting the forest industry which, as we all know, is the cornerstone of the economy of British Columbia and a very important part of the economy of Canada. The proposal by the federal Government on this issue reflects that reality.
Of course logging will continue to be one of the main industries in the Province of British Columbia and in Canada. But national parks, and the one we are talking about in particular, raise the prospect of a great new industry in British Columbia in the Queen Charlotte area, an industry based on a world-class tourist attraction and destination.
The example of the Pacific Rim National Park which I have mentioned frequently may be useful to consider. It has been identified by Tourism Canada as a superior tourist attraction. The park attracted more than 75 per cent of the visitors to the region in 1983. The estimated total spending of visitors to the region was more than $5.6 million. The benefits of this national park are material and immeasurable, as they are in all national parks.
South Moresby has the potential to become an international attraction for visitors to British Columbia if we seize the opportunity now. If an adequate part of that unique area is protected, as I have said, there will be an opportunity to develop this area into a first-class tourist destination. There are currently some 15 tour operators working in South Moresby, and further interest has been expressed by the small cruise ship market and other tourist operators. We can anticipate that this interest will continue to grow.
At one time, as one of the speakers said earlier, when the parks of Banff and Jasper were established in western Canada people wondered why government money was spent on these remote areas. I can tell Hon. Members that the tourists and the people of the world are pounding at the doors of these parks. There is scarcely any room in them. In order to find a place to stay for the night one has to be there early. At times, reservations have to be made ahead of time. These parks have become very popular places.
May 14, 1987

Thus when we look ahead, we have to base our cost figures on the potential of these parks in the future, because there will certainly be no more land and there will always be more people. Hon. Members can rest assured that places such as Jasper, Banff and other national parks in Canada will be recreated and re-experienced by a place such as South Moresby when a park is created there.
By way of example, tourism in the Pacific Rim Park has grown by an average of 60 per cent in each of the past five years. What a staggering growth that is! I am sure that the proposed park in South Moresby will experience the same type of attraction to tourists throughout the world. We expect that tourism in British Columbia will increase even more if a world-class national park is established in South Moresby. However, tour operators and those who know have said that the tourist potential will be greatly reduced if excessive logging, in particular logging on the south slopes of Lyell Island and other areas visible from the proposed park, continues. Therefore, I welcome the British Columbia offer as it appeared in today's newspapers which stated that it would discontinue logging immediately should an agreement be reached with respect to this park.
From a review of a number of recently established national parks in other countries which have also been designated as world heritage sites, and from discussion with UNESCO officials, it has been confirmed that the establishment and active promotion of a proposed South Moresby National Park and its designation as a world heritage site would result in attracting new visitors to the Queen Charlotte Islands, especially from international markets. Of course that was the example in such areas in Australia as the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park with which the whole world is now familiar. It has experienced an increase in attendance of 10 per cent per year since it was first established as a world heritage site. Certainly the site which is being proposed in the House this afternoon is no less an attraction than the Great Barrier Reef in and near Australia. Foreign visitors have played a significant role in that particular area. We expect them to play a very significant role in terms of the establishment of this park.
As we all know, last year British Columbia played host to the world through Expo. The world loved it. Tourism is turning out to be the main legacy of Expo 86. A world-class tourist destination in the Queen Charlotte Islands would make a continuing contribution to the province and to the Canadian economy.
According to the province, preliminary research has indicated that significant numbers of first-time visitors plan to return to British Columbia in order to fully explore that great and beautiful province. The tourism sector is optimistic about the future of post-Expo opportunities. The development of new products, such as cultural tourism and native cultural destinations, are considered significant new developments.
Supply
So quite aside from preserving the heritage of our beautiful country, there are very valid commercial reasons for proceeding with this proposal. We cannot ignore the commercial aspects of the proposal now before the House.
In the recent Speech from the Throne in the Legislature of British Columbia, we had an expression of the intention of the Province of British Columbia in respect of this proposal. In that speech, the Government of B.C. made the following statement:
We will attempt to expedite the federal-provincial negotiations for the establishment of a national park on South Moresby in the Queen Charlottes.
The speech went on:
My Government-
And that, of course, refers to the Social Credit Government of British Columbia:
My Government will seek a bilateral agreement with the federal government to develop the enormous tourism potential this area offers.
And the speech continued:
Working together, our two governments can create a national park and tourism environment that will not only generate major economic benefits for all British Columbia, but in particular, new employment and income for the friendly people of the Queen Charlottes region.
That is an objective, Mr. Speaker, that we share. I call upon the Government of British Columbia to carry through fully on that particular promise.
Today in this House we heard the commitment of the Minister to co-operate and to work hard toward the realization of that dream, a dream that has been around for many years. I call upon the Premier of the Province of British Columbia to match the Hon. Minister's enthusiasm.
I should like to take a moment to deal with another matter contained in the resolution, a matter which has been referred to on occasion this afternoon, that being the situation with respect to the Haida people.
I was pleased to hear both the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) and the Minister of the Environment indicate their commitment to the active involvement of the Haida in the planning and development and running of a national park reserve on South Moresby.
In closing, let me again congratulate the Hon. Member for Skeena on his motion. It is a subject that warrants the attention and support of all Members of the House. I am sure that we all share his desire and the desire of the Minister to see the establishment of a national park reserve in this area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to congratulate those who have preceded me in the

May 14, 1987
Adjournment Debate
debate, starting with the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer), the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), who comes from a beautiful province on the other side of the country, as well as the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), and the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight).
As a prairie boy, 1 support fully the efforts of all Hon. Members and the Government in the establishment of a national park reserve in the Queen Charlottes, and specifically the South Moresby area.
It is my hope that in the quest for an agreement, the loggers are not over-compensated. In my personal view, the compensation should amount to no more than the expenses involved in their departure from the area.
The trees of our wilderness areas belong to the people of Canada. Those companies involved in logging operations pay a royalty or stumpage fee on trees harvested. That is all they pay in order to harvest the forests of this country. Where a tree has not been harvested, no payment should be due the logger. But, in any event, let us get on with achieving agreement on this proposal for a national park reserve.
When it comes to the heritage of the environment, the resources, the natural habitat of this country, none of us have any right to leave a mess for succeeding generations.
Who do we think we are that we can waste our forests, pollute our waters, and foul our air in order to satisfy the bottom line syndrome, as I choose to call it, the principle of anything to make a buck? Since when does that take priority over the welfare of our people and our planet and our environment?
I hope that a national park reserve is no different from a national park. I am aware that in the case of some forest reserves, logging and mining interests have been allowed to operate. I am thinking of some reserve lands in eastern British Columbia and western Alberta, in the Rocky Mountains. These are what are called forest reserves and park reserves. Notwithstanding that they had been set aside as such, the regulations still permitted logging and mining operations.
I hope that in the establishment of the South Moresby National Park Reserve, no opening is left for the "cut-and-run" boys to move in down the road.
In supporting this proposal, I wish to take a moment to make an appeal for the establishment of the Grasslands National Park in southwestern Saskatchewan. This is something that the people of the Prairies, and particularly the people of Saskatchewan, have wanted for decades.
From my arrival here in 1968, there have been discussions and negotiations in respect of the Grasslands National Park. I can recall attending a large reception at which a profile map of
the entire park area was displayed. Agreement had been reached among the province and the federal Government, the local municipalities, the ranchers and other interests on the establishment of the Grasslands National Park. But, Mr. Speaker, we still do not have it. It is still not in place.
I suppose it could be called a place where the buffalo can roam and the deer and the antelope play, and groundhog and the sage grouse and the prairie dogs and rattlesnakes thrive. It could be a place where the original grasslands, and the Coulees, and the Badlands, and the Buttes can remain as they are and as they were.
I put in a plea that the Minister renew discussions on an urgent basis with the Government of Saskatchewan and any other interests on the establishment of the Grasslands National Park.
Saskatchewan is one of the few provinces still limited to one national park. Apart from the odd small area in the United States, the southwestern part of Saskatchewan is the only area where we still have the grasslands existing in their original state.
It is my hope that once the Hon. Minister has achieved agreement on the establishment of the South Moresby National Park Reserve, he will then turn his attention to getting established, once and for all, the Grasslands National Park in Saskatchewan. As far as both are concerned, he has the unanimous support of all Members from all sides of the House of Commons. That being said, let us now get it done.

subtopic: LITERACY-FUNCTIONALLY ILLITERATE ADULTS-NEED FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT SET DEADLINE FOR ENDING ILLITERACY
LITERACY-FUNCTIONALLY ILLITERATE ADULTS-NEED FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT SET DEADLINE FOR ENDING ILLITERACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 10 days ago I brought to the attention of the Government the fact that there are now five million functionally illiterate people in Canada and that their ability to find work in an
May 14, 1987

increasingly technological society is becoming smaller and smaller. I called upon the federal Government, in co-operation with the provinces, to develop a 10-year program with the objective to wipe out this blot on Canada.
I was appalled by the Minister's response, which simply promised more discussions and more meetings. There was little commitment, if any, to real action.
A substantial majority of the illiterate people in Canada were born in Canada. Almost half of them are under the age of 45 years. Some 60 per cent of them are unemployed and are not even looking for work. Given the 1.25 million unemployed at the present time, what chance would they have of being hired? Those who are lucky enough to obtain work are sentenced to minimum wage and uninteresting, mind-dulling work.
Who are the illiterate? They are farmers, native people, inmates in our jails and penitentiaries, and young people who somehow got through the school system without learning to read at a grade eight level or better. These five million people face a grim future for themselves, but their plight is creating an increasing danger for all Canadians.
However, the problem can be solved. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) announced a new program to tackle the problem of illiteracy among inmates in our prisons. I support the initiative but ask why we restrict the federal Government's involvement in the problem to our prisons.
Small successful programs have been operating in many parts of Canada. One of the most successful is Frontier College which has worked on this problem since the beginning of the century. In Ottawa, Calgary, Winnipeg, and other cities too numerous to mention, there are groups working with the illiterates in their areas. These groups were formed by churches, labour groups, and various community groups. They need the support of Governments, federal and provincial.
It has been demonstrated in Third World countries such as Cuba, China, and Venezuela that well planned programs which have the support of personnel and finances can succeed. Many of these countries have virtually wiped out illiteracy, which was so prevalent and was the fate of most of their people. If they can do it in Third World countries, we can do it in Canada.
These groups need support. They do not need to have plans worked out in Ottawa by the federal Government or even plans worked out in detail and imposed upon them by provincial Governments. The self-help groups need support, not only support of a financial nature. Their programs need publicity. They need more people involved and the development of new techniques. What they need the most is the assistance of thousands of volunteers who, I am convinced, would come forward to help in a very necessary program, if they were made aware of the need and were alerted to the kind of help they could provide in dealing with a tremendously serious problem.
Adjournment Debate
I call upon the federal Government to meet with the provincial and territorial Governments, to work out plans, and to set a timetable so that, if not in the 10 years which I suggested in my original questions, at least by the end of this century, the year 2000, we will no longer have to accept the reality that 20 per cent of the people living in Canada are still functionally illiterate.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: LITERACY-FUNCTIONALLY ILLITERATE ADULTS-NEED FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT SET DEADLINE FOR ENDING ILLITERACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I had more than three minutes because I think the Hon. Member knows that I am also interested in this subject.
In 1980 the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and I served on a task force which identified this problem and made certain recommendations to the federal Government at that time. I am pleased to note now that our Government is taking some action regarding adult literacy. Because of the encouragement of the committee headed by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), and its work, along with the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and myself, continued pressure has been put on cabinet Ministers to come forward with a literacy program.
The former Minister of the Environment sits there and laughs and makes fun, but it is a very serious problem. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North is absolutely right in what he says. The problem was recognized in the Speech from the Throne. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) are taking active roles. Last week the Secretary of State met with many of the country's leading experts in the field of literacy. Among them were representatives of the Movement for Canadian Literacy, Laubach Literacy of Canada, Regroupement des Groupes Populaires en Alphabetisation, the Canadian Business Task Force on Literacy and the International Council for Adult Education. It was made clear at that time to the delegates that the Government does, indeed, recognize the problem and that it is taking a very active role. Another meeting will be held shortly, and the Minister will be presenting some information that I think Canadians will appreciate very much.
We are fully aware of the fact that illiteracy is costly in personal, educational, social and economic terms. The Member is correct that the volunteer sector is very important. It is the key to the whole program. I spent some time with the Peel Literacy Guild on Appreciation Night. Labour, industry and the volunteers-of which we have a large number in Peel but we can always use more-were honoured.
What the Secretary of State is doing at present, in cooperation with other Governments and organizations-because 1 think it has to be a co-operative effort-is trying to identify short-term initiatives immediately but in parallel with longterm strategies for lasting solutions. We have started with one of those short-term initiatives by increasing the basic adult literacy program among federal penitentiary inmates. This will

May 14, 1987
Adjournment Debate
increase the number of inmates who will be taught reading and writing. It will be established over the next three years, with an increase of 400 per cent in the number of inmates receiving this type of training. That is just a start on what I and this Government consider a very serious problem. There will be more action in the very near future.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-WHEAT FARMERS 1987-88 CROP YEAR-REQUEST FOR DEFICIENCY PAYMENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW DEBT RESTRUCTURING INSTRUMENTS
AGRICULTURE-WHEAT FARMERS 1987-88 CROP YEAR-REQUEST FOR DEFICIENCY PAYMENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW DEBT RESTRUCTURING INSTRUMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday of this week I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) as a result of his trip to western Canada. I asked him whether after four days in the west he would decide to finally provide a deficiency payment for the new crop year, 1987-88.
The Prime Minister met, albeit with selected people- mostly partisan supporters of his own-but even in meeting with a very select group of partisan supporters the message was always the same, that the situation in southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba needed a commitment by the Government for the new crop year.
It is unfortunate that the Prime Minister refused to meet with the western wheat pools, the prairie pools and their constituent organizations, the National Farmers Union and the Keystone Agricultural groups. The Prime Minister when in the west operated on a solely photo-opportunity, closed-shop type of basis. It may have impressed people in eastern Canada that the Prime Minister was meeting with people in agriculture who are facing the worst economic crisis since the 1930s, but it did not impress the westerners themselves.
On Monday, May 11, the Montreal Gazette said the Prime Minister's message in the west missed the mark. The paper goes on to outline how the Prime Minister met with some Party supporters but did not get down to meeting with the broad-based agricultural groups who are facing such a difficult time. On May 9, The Globe and Mail said the Prime Minister's western trip generated scant enthusiasm. On May 10 the Sunday Sun reported that the welcome for the Prime Minister was lukewarm to hostile.
On Monday I asked whether or not the Prime Minister would make a commitment to a deficiency payment. The general strategy of the Government has been to keep talking about what assistance was provided in the current crop year, without making a firm commitment. The decrease in farm income is calculated at $2 billion to $3 billion from the 198586 crop year, yet we have no commitment from the Prime Minister. I believe he will be meeting with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on May 29. At this stage it appears that meeting will only be about an hour, a quick snapshot visit with the producers. The producers do not want the Minister of Agriculture to do what he did a few months ago, walk into the meeting, throw down a press release and say "this is what we are issuing as a result of this meeting".
The second part of my question dealt with the terrible financial crisis facing agriculture right across the country. It has been estimated that the value of farmland has decreased by some $17 billion since this Government came to power in September, 1984. There are about 170,000 economic-sized farms with gross sales of at least $20,000 a year. That means each of those farmers have lost an average of $100,000 in land value. When the Prime Minister talks about assistance amounting to $2 billion or $3 billion over the last couple of years, we have to compare it with the amount farmers have lost.
I asked the Prime Minister if he would make a commitment to bring in new debt restructuring instruments which would assist some 52,000 farmers who are facing either total insolvency or serious cash flow problems. His response was that he would be looking into it, but he made no firm commitment. That was a tremendous disappointment to every western farmer, indeed every farmer in the country. The Prime Minister went out there, he saw the malaise, hardship, indeed the tortured unfairness of it all. Farmers in this country are not receiving the same level of support as those in the U.S.
Thousands of our youngest and most productive farmers are facing the loss of their land and there are no proper debt restructuring instruments being put in place. The ones which are there are totally inadequate for the circumstances of the day.
I certainly hope that the Government will move expeditiously on both of these problems. We want a commitment now that farmers will receive an adequate deficiency payment in the new crop year this fall and that new debt restructuring instruments and programs will be put in place to assist farmers to stay on the land and continue to produce the food that is vitally needed for this country and for our international commitments.

Mir. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to complete what was said by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his answer to this question on May 11 this year.
The Government sees agriculture as a very important industry, a position that was reflected in the Prime Minister's pertinent and enlightened replies. The Government realizes that grain producers have been severely affected by the dramatic drop in world prices for grain, caused by a subsidy war between the European Economic Community and the United States.
We also realize that Western Canada has been particularly affected, and that is why we have taken exceptional measures to deal with this situation. Since we came to power, financial assistance to western farmers through federal programs has more than tripled. For this year alone, direct payments to
May 14, 1987

farmers under federal programs are expected to increase by about $1 billion over last year's, making a total of about $3 billion.
Mr. Speaker, to be perfectly frank, I think this is more than just lip service. These are concrete measures. They are official measures. These measures are the national expression of a national party, the Progressive Conservative Party, and were taken by our Prime Minister, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) together with all provincial Agriculture Ministers, who represent four Parties between them, and they all agreed to help western farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) may not fully understand the problem because his speech does not recognize the facts, it does not recognize that we are fully aware of what is going on, we are fully aware of the steps taken by our Minister of Agriculture, the Prime Minister, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board to help Western producers cope through cash payments, we are thinking of the coming stabilization payments, $702 million, $64 million extra payments that have just been announced to help pay freight rates. We are aware that under those policies we are putting in place to help Canadian agriculture, we must keep on co-operating with the farming industry, we must keep on working with provinces to finally give farming something decent, a stable role, a foundation within our economy, our economic activity.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress to my colleague for Algoma that the Prime Minister is aware of farmers' problems, that he is the first Prime Minister in Canadian history who has ever succeeded in making agriculture a priority on the GATT agenda. That is a tangible move by this Government because agriculture is important to us, both in words and in deeds.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-NIAGARA RIVER CLEAN-UP PLAN. (B) START OF OPERATIONS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-NIAGARA RIVER CLEAN-UP PLAN. (B) START OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raised dealt with the Niagara River toxic problem and particularly with the management plan which was formulated to clean up the toxic chemicals which enter the Niagara River through municipal and industrial sewers and seep from old toxic chemical dumps through the porous bedrock directly into the river from the United States side. More details on how this plan will be defined, hopefully including targets, deadlines and a commitment to zero discharge, are to be released in July of this year.
Now, however, there is a wrench in the works and an open flank in the battle plan. It concerns airborne chemicals. The Niagara work plan agreed to in February of this year did not address the possibility of toxic chemicals being released into
Adjournment Debate
the air at Niagara Falls. This is a major blunder that could have been prevented.
In 1984, Dr. Barry Oliver, at the Canada Centre for Inland Waters in Burlington, calculated that 50 per cent of the toxic chemicals in the Niagara River volatilized, that is left the water by way of vapours and entered the air at the Falls themselves. Dr. Oliver wanted to measure toxic chemicals in the mist in 1984, but the severe cuts that were inflicted in November, 1984, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and subsequent budgets of Environment Canada made it impossible for Dr. Oliver to receive the money or the help to pursue this research. Finally, Dr. Oliver left Environment Canada in February of this year.
When the blob in the St. Clair River occurred, its clean-up sapped the limited resources that Environment Canada had left to respond to chemical crises.
In October, 1986, Pollution Probe did what Environment Canada should have done. They took samples of the mist at Niagara Falls and found nine toxic chemicals, including chloroform, benzene and toluene, in small amounts, that are not immediate health threats but could pose a chronic, longterm health hazard.
Last week came the release of the study done by Donald MacKay and Michael McLachlan, of the University of Toronto, which indicated that 35 to 175 tonnes of chemicals go into the air each year at Niagara Falls.
The questions that emerge are fundamental. Why has Environment Canada been so reduced in its capacity and strength to study toxic chemicals that only one full-time scientist is working on the Niagara River Toxics Management Plan while Ontario has four people on site?
Why was Dr. Oliver not provided with the necessary funds to carry out the study at the Falls in relation to the plan that had been conceived in recent times and would have included the study of toxicity released at the Falls themselves? Will Environment Canada, belatedly and after many warnings, tackle the problems of toxic chemicals in the mist at Niagara Falls? Finally, Environment Canada must get heavily involved at the Falls in measuring these toxics. Otherwise, how accurate can the estimates be of toxic chemical loadings based on measurements at Fort Erie and Niagara-on-the-Lake?
We are talking about the health of millions of Canadians in the Niagara Peninsula. We are also talking about the viability of the tourist industry, which is very intense, with millions of visitors every year. We must ensure that the issue is handled and that we know the impact of the toxic chemicals that are released at the Falls. We must ensure the presence of Environment Canada in international waters because that is demanded of the Department. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will give us a satisfactory answer.

Mr. Speaker, all of my answers are

May 14, 1987
Adjournment Debate
satisfactory so I do not know why the Hon. Member would add that caveat to his presentation.
I might say that there have been many solid achievements in the Niagara River issue. Of course, it is a major issue and one that should concern us all. Being an Ontarian and a Bramp-tonian who gets water from Lake Ontario, naturally I should be very interested in the issue. As a parliamentarian, I spent the weekend in Niagara Falls. A more beautiful part of the world is hard to find. There is no question about that.
The Hon. Member talked about the Niagara River Toxics Management Plan which had been agreed upon by Canada, Ontario, the United States and New York, and the second major initiative on February 4, 1987, of an international declaration of intent which is intended to accompany and complement the Niagara River Toxics Management Plan. This is a very important document because it talks about the political will to support the toxics management plan and to work toward what I think is key, the reduction of loadings to toxic chemicals entering the Niagara River by 50 per cent over the coming decade.
1 think that is a great goal to work toward. I hope they surpass it as, I am sure, does the Hon. Member. I think we all do. We have the political will now. The Hon. Member knows how difficult it was to get that political will. He is a former Minister of the Environment and he had his problems getting those agreements signed. He should be happy that the political will is there now and that we have to get on with the job.
With respect to the toxics in the air to which the Hon. Member referred, there have been some media reports about this matter. By the way, the Hon. Member asked this question last November and is just following up now. I find that interesting. There have been recent media reports relating to a University of Toronto modelling study. The model estimated quantities of volatile chemicals evaporating into the air from the Niagara River and Niagara Falls.
This particular study was supported by Environment Canada on the basis that previous research conducted by the Government provided indications of the volatile nature of some of the contaminates carried in the river. So we have been involved in that right from the start, and we support it. While the model predictions should be considered preliminary-and the Hon. Member will understand that-and speculative at this time, support of such work is indicative of the continuing efforts by Canada to investigate and describe the environmental pathways, fate and effects of chemical contaminates in this system. Environment Canada will be conducting further research on volatile chemicals at Niagara Falls this year.
The Hon. Member tells us that Ontario has four people on site and we only have one person on site. I can tell the Hon. Member that that has been one of the major problems with the Government of Canada, trying to outdo the Ontario Government or vice versa. The money all comes from the same pocket. The important thing is that work is going on there now and we are studying this particular problem. It is worrisome to us all. It is being investigated.
Now that we have the political will, I think that is about three quarters of the battle won. We can now get on with the toxics management plan, together with the declaration of intent, which is intended to push the parties toward the goal of zero discharge and virtual elimination in a scheduled and stepwise fashion, which I think is very important. I think we should congratulate the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for the work he has done.
